chapter: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
title: Duke on avant-garde records, and Ornette's confident upbringing
summary: Ellington declines to go back to avant-garde; Mingus contrasts Ornette's parented confidence with his own struggle for approval.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: I have to tell you about what Duke has done. Like, I asked Duke, when are we going to make that record, Clark Terry, Dan Jones, myself and you and some you want, to make a real avant garde record?
Yeah.
He said, Mingus, let's not go back that far. Let's do something up to date, like you and me and Max Roach (inaudible).
Yeah.
We don't need to prove nothing.
Did you ever get a chance to --
Because -- wait a minute, man, you know what that means?
Yeah.

Red Norvo said one good thing in his life. When he first heard some kids playing, he said, it reminds me of some kids, you give them some blocks, and Mama says he can do anything he wants to do with them, stack them up this way and that way, and they say, look, Mommy, what I've done.
Yeah.
Ornette Coleman must have had the nicest mother in the world. Everything he does he plays it so nice and beautiful.
Yeah.
I never had that. Nobody never said nothing about my music being good, that's why I keep trying all the time.
Yeah.
Those guys that are out there, like Buddy Bluitt, their parents told them they was good.
Yeah.
They got a lot of confidence in what they do. They don't have to do anything simple. I had to do something simple to make sense to myself.
So that kind of overindulgence by the parent is not necessarily the best training. If that's the way it worked. Came too easy, for them, I mean.
Yeah. I'm sure that's what they had, though, man.
That's funny, though.
(Unintelligible) and the mother said, I don't know, son, better write another one. I don't know how good that one is.
